extracted.intended_audience: English-language newspaper readers interested in European affairs and supporters of Italian republican/liberal causes
extracted.subtask_description: Contemporary journalistic dispatch describing the Siege of Rome (June–July 1849), including battlefield events, civilian conditions, proclamations/edicts, and a circulated Address instructing civic resistance. Written for general readers of a periodical concerned with European politics and humanitarian consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address to the People of Rome — recommended conduct (civil noncooperation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescriptive guidelines circulated to Romans advising a program of noncooperation and dignified silence: “Silence is the weapon we have now to use against the Cossacks of France and the priests... In the streets do not look at them; do not answer if they address you. In the cafés, in the eating-houses, if they enter, rise and go out. Let your windows remain closed as they pass. Never attend their feasts, their parades. Regard the harmony of their musical bands as tones of slavery... And you, Roman women, masterpiece of God's work! deign no look, no smile, to those satellites of an abhorred Pope!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: peaceful civic resistance and moral isolation of occupying forces; concrete actions include looking away, not speaking, leaving cafés, keeping windows shut, refusing to attend entertainments, and using the repeated cry ‘VIVA LA REPUBLICA!’ as a unifying refrain. The Address frames these acts as both civic duty and moral demonstration; it includes social sanctions (public naming/execration of those who fraternize) and stresses sustained constancy despite reprisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martial-law edicts and occupier-imposed rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported occupier proclamations and enforced rules: “the press is stifled; everybody is to be in the house at half past nine o'clock in the evening, and whoever in any way insults his men, or puts any obstacle in their way, is to be shot.” Also: edicts to disarm the National Guard; to take down Republican insignia as “emblems of anarchy;” and an order commanding all foreigners who had been in the service of the Republican government to leave Rome within twenty-four hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are procedural requirements imposed by the French commanders as instruments of control: curfew, suppression of the press, capital punishment for perceived insults or obstruction, disarmament of civic forces, removal of symbols, and rapid expulsion of foreign supporters. The report notes the practical and humanitarian consequences (loss of civic freedom, hardship for wounded and foreigners) and frames these edicts as indications of occupier intent and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection (and violation) of hospitals and monuments as a moral standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit standard asserted in the reportage: occupying forces ought to avoid harming hospitals and priceless monuments; the article condemns bombs falling on the chief hospital and apparent aiming at the Capitol, and documents later French appropriation/misuse of hospital space (driving away nurses, moving wounded to an airless granary, occupying good wards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: conduct of war should spare medical facilities and cultural heritage; violations are presented as especially barbarous and morally culpable. The piece uses specific examples (bombs on hospitals, damage to St. Maria Trastevere, appropriation of Quirinal and Palazzo di Venezia courtyards) to illustrate the breach and to strengthen the moral indictment of the occupiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilian bomb-response and rescue practices (extinguishing bombs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive-prescriptive examples of effective civilian countermeasures to incendiary bombs: individuals (including a Trasteverini woman and a soldier) seized bombs and extinguished the matches, using pans of wet clay to run to bomb-fall sites and put out incendiaries; such acts were rewarded (medals, promotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance and social encouragement: immediate action to extinguish bombs minimizes loss of life and is worthy of public recognition; examples function both as model behavior and as encouragement for communal courage and mutual aid during bombardment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities and conduct valorized for defenders and volunteers (republican virtues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative criteria for what constitutes 'respectable' defenders: self-sacrifice, voluntary service, readiness to risk wealth and comfort for liberty, steadfastness in the face of defeat — exemplified by Garibaldi's volunteers, students, exiles, and 'the flower of the Italian youth.' The author contrasts this with contempt for those who label such men 'brigands' or 'vagabonds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a moral-evaluative standard used throughout the dispatch to judge actors: bravery, devotion, and willingness to sacrifice are praised and presented as the true markers of respectability; conversely, passive material comfort and collaboration with occupiers are negatively judged. The rhetoric serves to legitimize the Republican cause and to shape reader sympathy.
